name: Medpor chin implant

lead: Medpor is a high-density porous polyethylene used for chin implants. It is one of the three common synthetic chin materials, alongside silicone and ePTFE.
It is discussed in looksmaxxing as a hardmaxx way to add chin projection. Published evidence in the reviewed material is thin, mostly technique descriptions.

paras: A shaped implant is placed over the chin bone; tissue grows into its pores, anchoring it and supporting blood supply [1].

General risks of chin implants include swelling, hematoma, temporary numbness, infection, displacement and nerve damage. Porous implants are described as harder to remove because tissue grows into them.

studies.title: Modified technique of chin augmentation with MEDPOR for Asian patients.

lead: A Medpor chin implant is a chin augmentation implant made of high-density porous polyethylene, a hard, porous and slightly flexible material. Tissue grows into its pores, which anchors it and supports blood supply, but also makes it harder to remove than non-porous alternatives [1]. It is one of several alloplastic (synthetic) options alongside silicone and expanded PTFE [1][2].

In looksmaxxing it is categorised as a hardmaxxing option for chin projection. Published material on it is limited; one plastic-surgery paper describes a modified technique for Asian patients, in which the outer aspect of the implant is reshaped to create an appropriate chin shape [2].

paras: Commonly used chin implants are made of silicone, expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE) or high-density porous polyethylene [2]. A general reference describes the porous polyethylene type as hard and slightly flexible, with tissue growth into the pores acting as anchorage and supporting blood supply, with the trade-off that removal is more difficult [1].

A 2012 paper in Aesthetic Surgery Journal describes Medpor as an effective implant for chin augmentation, but recommends modification of its external aspect, particularly in Asian patients, to create an appropriate shape for the new chin. It notes that it can be difficult to contour the inner aspect of the implant to conform to the patient's mandible, and that without modification a gap may result [2].

General risks of alloplastic chin implants listed in a reference work include swelling, hematoma, temporary lip weakness or numbness, and less commonly infection, implant displacement and nerve damage [1]. Ease of removal is described as lower for porous implants than for non-porous ones [1].

The surgical literature reviewed here contains a single descriptive paper on a modified Medpor chin augmentation technique for Asian patients [2]. No randomised or comparative trials of Medpor against other chin implants were found in the material reviewed.
